Title: High-level microwave disinfection of dental gypsum casts.

Journal/Date: The International journal of prosthodontics (2005)

MeSH Keywords: Alginates, Calcium Sulfate, Colony Count, Microbial, Dental Disinfectants, Dental Impression Materials, Disinfection, Microwaves, Models, Dental


--- ABSTRACT ---
[PURPOSE]: To test whether microwave oven irradiation can disinfect gypsum casts in compliance with current disinfection requirements, and to determine whether this procedure would be as effective as a validated method of chemical disinfection of impressions.
[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: In 2 in vitro experiments, samples of 5 irreversible hydrocolloid impressions of a disinfected acrylic resin model were contaminated with suspensions of recommended test organisms Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, respectively. In 1 in vivo experiment, 10 impressions were made of 10 subjects. All impressions were poured and the resulting casts cut in 2 halves. One half of each cast was exposed to 5 minutes of irradiation in a microwave oven at 2,450 MHz and 900 W. The other halves were left untreated as controls. In a second in vivo experiment, 10 impressions were disinfected by immersion in a 0.07% solution of NaOCl at pH of about 10 for 3 minutes, and then poured. All casts were incubated aerobically in Bacto tryptic soy broth at 37 degrees C for 6 hours and assessed for bacterial growth by counting colony-forming units per milliliter (cfu/mL) of the culture. The results were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
[RESULTS]: Untreated gypsum casts showed cfu/mL counts with a median log value of 6, while microwave-irradiated ones had median cfu/mL counts of 0. Casts poured from chemically disinfected impressions demonstrated cfu/mL counts with a median log value of 4.
[CONCLUSION]: Under the described conditions, microwave-irradiated gypsum casts satisfy current disinfection requirements, but gypsum casts poured from chemically disinfected impressions do not.

[BACKGROUND]: One of the major problems of everyday dental practice is cross-contamination. It can place office personnel, dentists, and patients at risk of acquiring serious illness. Disinfection helps in controlling this cross-contamination to an extent. The evaluation was done to find the efficient disinfection method on gypsum casts.
[AIMS]: The aim of this study is to evaluate and compare the efficacy of three methods of disinfection of gypsum casts, namely, chemical disinfection by immersion, spray method, and microwave method, and also to evaluate and compare changes in surface roughness and dimensional accuracy between the three methods after disinfection.
[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: Ex vivo and experimental study. Thirty participants were selected, and impressions of the maxillary arch were made using polyvinyl siloxane impression material. Ninety type IV die stone gypsum casts were poured. It was divided into three groups and was subjected to chemical disinfection by immersion and spray methods, and microwave method. The disinfected casts were evaluated for microbial growth, surface roughness, and dimensional accuracy. It was performed by using the one-way analysis of variance test and paired t-test followed by the Kruskal - Wallis test and Wilcoxon signed rank test (α = 0.05).
[RESULTS]: Microwave disinfection was more effective than both immersion and spray chemical disinfection methods (P < 0.010 and <0.001). The surface roughness of the microwave-irradiated casts had significantly increased after disinfection. However, there were no significant dimensional changes by any of the methods of disinfection.
[CONCLUSION]: Within the limitations of the study, the microwave method of disinfection is more effective in eradicating microorganisms when compared to chemical methods of disinfection by immersion and spray methods.

key_findings.finding: A direct head-to-head comparison does exist. In a 2005 study, gypsum casts were microwaved at 2,450 MHz/900 W for 5 minutes versus casts poured from impressions immersed in 0.07% NaOCl (pH ~10) for 3 minutes; median log10 CFU/mL was 0 for microwave-treated casts versus 4 for the chemically disinfected group and 6 for untreated controls. Under those conditions, microwave treatment met disinfection requirements whereas chemical treatment did not. This compares treatment of the cast with disinfection of the impression before pouring, so it is not a perfectly like-for-like cast intervention.

A 2014 in-vitro study directly evaluated contaminated Type III dental-stone casts: microwave irradiation for 5 minutes at 900 W versus 0.5% sodium hypochlorite chemical disinfection. Against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, both treatments produced approximately a 5-log10 CFU/mL reduction and were reported as equivalent and compliant with laboratory infection-control requirements. The abstract does not report dimensional accuracy, surface detail, hardness, or strength.

source_tools.relevance: Exact microwave protocol, chemical agent, and comparative CFU outcome

key_findings.finding: A 2013 laboratory study compared microwave energy levels with sodium hypochlorite concentrations using inoculated dental-stone carriers and CFU/mL outcomes. Microwave treatment at 600 W for 3 minutes achieved high-level disinfection; immersion in 0.06% sodium hypochlorite for 2 minutes achieved disinfection, described as similar to a validated chemical method. This was a parameter-comparison study rather than a full cast-property comparison.

source_tools.relevance: Exact microwave and NaOCl conditions and microbial endpoint

key_findings.finding: A 2024 ex-vivo study of 90 Type IV die-stone casts compared chemical immersion, chemical spray, and microwave disinfection, assessing microbial growth, surface roughness, and dimensional accuracy. Microwave treatment was more effective microbiologically than both chemical methods (P<0.010 and P<0.001), significantly increased surface roughness, and none of the methods caused significant dimensional change. The PubMed abstract does not specify microwave power/time or the chemical agent, and it does not report hardness or strength.

source_tools.relevance: Most relevant recent cast study with microbial, roughness, and dimensional outcomes

key_findings.finding: A 2025 Type IV dental-stone study compared 0.5% chlorhexidine, 0.5% sodium hypochlorite, 20% neem extract, and microwave irradiation for 1–5 minutes using biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus mutans, and Candida albicans; CFU counts and scanning electron microscopy were used. Chlorhexidine, sodium hypochlorite, and microwave significantly reduced CFU; neem was less potent. Microwave and NaOCl had similar potency against C. albicans, while organism-specific differences favored CHX or NaOCl/microwave in some comparisons. Microwave wattage and immersion/contact details are not stated in the abstract, and no dimensional accuracy, roughness, hardness, or strength outcomes are reported.

source_tools.relevance: Recent direct comparison with multiple chemicals, organisms, and SEM endpoint

key_findings.finding: Property studies provide adjunct evidence but not chemical comparisons: 600 W for 3 minutes after repeated wetting increased diametral tensile strength of Type III and IV stone without changing compressive strength; the study did not include a chemical-disinfectant arm. Thus, published evidence addresses strength after microwave exposure, but comparative microwave-versus-chemical evidence for hardness/strength or surface detail is insufficient.
